question: A screening test for tuberculosis has sensitivity 80% and specificity 95%. When applied to a high-prevalence urban slum population (prevalence 5%) versus a low-prevalence rural population (prevalence 0.5%), what happens to the Positive Predictive Value (PPV)?

answers.text: PPV increases as prevalence decreases because fewer false positives occur

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In fact, as prevalence falls, the number of true positives drops sharply while false positives persist, so PPV falls — not rises.

answers.text: PPV remains unchanged because sensitivity and specificity are fixed properties of the test

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sensitivity and specificity are test properties, but PPV also depends on prevalence. The same test in a low-prevalence population yields a much lower PPV.

answers.text: PPV is higher in the high-prevalence population because there are more true positives relative to false positives

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. PPV = TP / (TP + FP). As prevalence rises, TP increases while FP (driven by specificity) stays proportional to true negatives. Hence PPV improves with higher prevalence — a key Wilson-Jungner point.

answers.text: PPV depends only on specificity, not on prevalence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PPV depends on both specificity AND prevalence. High specificity reduces false positives, but low prevalence still dilutes PPV by swamping true positives with false ones.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key principle: PPV rises with disease prevalence. In a low-prevalence population, even an excellent test generates many false positives relative to true positives, making PPV poor.
Excellent. This is why population-wide screening is only recommended when prevalence is high enough that PPV is acceptable — a core Wilson-Jungner criterion.
